turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_retention_train.csv: 55 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S) and `target` (the measured hot-strength retention ratio
    YS(600C)/YS(20C)).
  - b3_htsteel_retention_pool.csv: 26 CANDIDATE samples whose hot-strength
    retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C) was NOT measured, columns
    `candidate_id` and the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST hot-
strength retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C), then select the 5 best candidates
from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
The training observations with the highest measured retention ratios fall into a small number of distinct composition families:

- Ni-base / Fe-Ni alloys containing substantial W + Ti + Al (targets 1.00, 0.875, 0.821).  
- A very low-alloy 0.5 Mo steel (target 0.937).  
- A high-Ti Fe-Ni alloy (target 0.903).  

All other families present in the training set (plain C-Mn, 12 % Cr, 18-8, high-Mn-V, etc.) give distinctly lower ratios (typically 0.3–0.77).

Direct nearest-neighbour matching of the 26 candidates onto these families yields a clear ranking:

- c019 is essentially identical to the two highest-Ni + W + Ti + Al alloys and is therefore expected to be the single best.  
- c015 is compositionally almost indistinguishable from the 0.937 Mo steel.  
- c011 matches the 0.903 high-Ti alloy (minor differences in Ni/Mo are second-order).  
- c013 is the same Ni–Ti–Al–W base as the 0.821 alloy plus extra Mo, hence still high but below the three preceding points.  
- c004 is the same base without W, placing it fifth.

No other candidate lies close to any training point whose target exceeds ~0.77.

Final: c019, c015, c011, c013, c004
